title: Grade 7 Science — Mon, Jun 23
description: Heat — Day 1 of 5: Temperature, thermometers, heat vs temperature
subject: science

questions.question: What is the difference between heat and temperature?
options: Heat is a form of energy (measured in Joules); temperature is the measure of hotness or coldness of an object (measured in °C or K)
Temperature is energy; heat is a scale
Heat is measured in °C; temperature in Joules
questions.explanation: Heat = thermal energy transferred from a hotter to a cooler object (unit: Joule). Temperature = degree of hotness or coldness (unit: °C or Kelvin). A large body can have more heat than a small body even at the same temperature.

questions.question: The instrument used to measure temperature is:
questions.explanation: Thermometer measures temperature. Barometer = air pressure. Hygrometer = humidity. Voltmeter = electric potential difference.

questions.question: Normal human body temperature is approximately:
questions.explanation: Normal human body temperature ≈ 37°C (98.6°F). Clinical (doctor's) thermometers are designed to read in the range 35°C to 42°C. Above 40°C indicates high fever.

questions.question: A clinical thermometer has a kink (constriction) near the bulb. Why?
options: To prevent mercury from falling back into the bulb after reading — the kink breaks the mercury thread so the temperature reading is retained
To make it easier to hold
questions.explanation: The kink/constriction prevents mercury from flowing back when you remove the thermometer from the body — the reading is preserved. Laboratory thermometers have no kink (mercury falls back), suitable for continuous reading.

questions.question: Heat always flows from:
options: Hotter object to colder object, until both reach the same temperature
questions.explanation: Heat flows spontaneously from HOT → COLD until thermal equilibrium (both at same temperature). This is the Second Law of Thermodynamics in simple terms. Cold doesn't flow; only heat (energy) flows.

questions.question: Which thermometer would a doctor use to check a patient's body temperature?
questions.explanation: Clinical thermometer: range 35–42°C (covers the human body temperature range), has a kink to hold the reading, sterile, safe mercury or digital. Laboratory thermometer has a wider range and no kink.

questions.question: Why should you not shake a clinical thermometer without checking it is pointing downward first?
options: Mercury might accidentally enter your mouth if the thermometer is used orally
questions.explanation: Mercury is toxic. Before use, the mercury must be shaken back below 35°C. Hold it firmly at the opposite end to the bulb, shake downward. Accidental mercury ingestion or spillage is a health hazard.

questions.question: The Celsius scale is defined so that: 0°C = ___ and 100°C = ___
options: Boiling point of water, Freezing point of water
Freezing point of pure water at sea level (ice point), Boiling point of pure water at sea level (steam point)
Melting point of ice in salt, Boiling point of salt water
questions.explanation: Celsius scale fixed points: 0°C = freezing/melting point of pure water at 1 atm pressure. 100°C = boiling point of pure water at 1 atm pressure. 100 equal divisions between these points.

questions.question: Two cups of tea: one at 80°C with 500 mL, one at 80°C with 200 mL. Which has more HEAT?
options: 500 mL cup (more thermal energy even at same temperature)
questions.explanation: Same temperature (80°C) but different amounts of matter. The 500 mL cup contains more molecules vibrating at the same speed → more total thermal energy (heat). Temperature measures average kinetic energy per particle; heat is the total thermal energy.

questions.question: A maximum-minimum thermometer is used to:
options: Record both the highest and lowest temperatures reached over a time period — useful in weather stations
questions.explanation: Maximum-minimum thermometer (Six's thermometer) uses two liquid columns to record the highest temperature (max) and lowest temperature (min) reached since it was last reset. Used in greenhouses, weather monitoring.

questions.question: Convert 37°C to Kelvin: (K = °C + 273)
questions.explanation: K = °C + 273 = 37 + 273 = 310 K. Absolute zero (0 K) = −273°C — theoretically the coldest possible temperature. Water boils at 373 K (100°C).

questions.question: Why is mercury used in thermometers? (Choose the BEST answer)
options: It expands uniformly with temperature, doesn't wet glass, is opaque and easily visible, and has a wide liquid range (−39°C to 357°C)
It is the only liquid metal
questions.explanation: Mercury is ideal because: (1) Uniform expansion. (2) Doesn't stick to glass (non-wetting). (3) Shiny silver colour, easy to read. (4) Wide liquid range. Disadvantage: toxic — modern thermometers increasingly use coloured alcohol or digital sensors.

questions.question: If you hold ice in your hand, your hand feels cold because:
options: Cold flows from the ice to your hand
Heat flows FROM your hand TO the ice — your hand loses energy, which is detected as a cold sensation
Your nerves produce a cold feeling
questions.explanation: Cold is NOT a form of energy that flows. Heat always flows from hot (hand at 37°C) to cold (ice at 0°C). Your hand loses heat to the ice → nerves detect the temperature drop as cold. The sensation of cold = absence of heat.

questions.question: A laboratory thermometer and a clinical thermometer — key structural difference:
options: Laboratory thermometer has no kink (mercury falls back — for continuous reading); clinical has a kink (mercury held at peak reading)
questions.explanation: Lab thermometer: no kink, mercury returns after removal from heat source, range −10 to 110°C. Clinical: kink retains peak reading, range 35–42°C. The kink is the clinical thermometer's essential design feature.

questions.question: Thermal equilibrium means:
options: One object is hotter than the other
Two objects in contact reach the same temperature and heat transfer stops
Heat is produced equally by both objects
Temperature is the same as heat
questions.explanation: Thermal equilibrium: when two objects in thermal contact reach the same temperature — net heat flow stops. This is the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics: if A is in equilibrium with B, and B with C, then A is in equilibrium with C.
